tagline: Through working forest country, past a lake protected from development
intro: Flat Tops Trail connects Meeker and Yampa across 82 miles of ranches, mines and timber-producing woodlands. Gravel County Road 8 crosses Ripple Creek Pass, where an overlook south of the summit faces the Flat Tops and its wilderness area. This is a Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway and a National Forest Scenic Byway. CDOT credits the landscape’s scenic and wildlife appeal to its combination of preservation and multiple-use land management. CDOT gives the crossing a two-hour driving time. Winter closures interrupt the through route at both ends of the mountain section.

The route passes through the original White River Plateau Timberland Reserve, set aside in the late nineteenth century. At Trappers Lake, the Forest Service hired Arthur Carhart to survey a road around the water. His recommendation led to the area being put largely off limits to development in 1920, the first Forest Service property protected in that manner. The larger Flat Tops Wilderness Area received its designation in 1975.

Begin in Meeker’s wide White River valley. Trappers Lake lies east of Meeker and west of Yampa, a separate excursion into the wilderness area. Ripple Creek Pass carries the byway across the boundary between White River and Routt national forests. Yampa completes the crossing at the route’s eastern end.

moments.title: Meeker
moments.text: Meeker is a ranching community on the north side of the White River, at the base of a long ridge. The annual Meeker Classic Sheepdog trials are held here. When Meeker was a prominent stagecoach stop, Rueben Sanford Ball built its brick hotel in 1896, using materials brought by freight wagon from Rifle. East and west wings added in 1904 expanded it to forty rooms. The historic hotel remains standing. The stone building now housing the café began as the town’s post office in 1891, then became a bank before the café moved there in 1918.

moments.title: Trappers Lake
moments.text: The large semicircle of the Amphitheater rises among the Flat Tops Mountains surrounding Trappers Lake. The lake sits at 9,633 feet and stretches roughly a mile and a half. In 1920, the area became the first Forest Service property put largely off limits to development, following Arthur Carhart’s recommendation after he was hired to survey a road around it. Fire later changed the surrounding forest: lightning started the Big Fish wildfire in July 2002, burning about 17,000 acres near the lake. The protected lake now lies within the Flat Tops Wilderness Area, in White River National Forest.
moments.notice: The Amphitheater forms a large semicircle among the mountains surrounding the lake.

moments.title: Yampa
moments.text: Yampa takes its name from the Northern Ute word for the Perideridia root, an important food source. The town’s growing season typically averages just 80 days. Just east of town, the Bear River joins the Yampa River. That tributary starts in the Flat Tops Wilderness above Stillwater Reservoir, connecting this end of the drive to the mountain country upstream.

practical: Meeker: The byway closes in winter on the west at approximately mile 31 and on the east at Dunkley Pass. Roads become muddy when wet. (checked 2026-10-11)
